note:
One sent out as an eyewitness of the resurrected Christ and as His official representative (2 Cor. 1:1 note).

**by the will of God.** Paul identifies the one who commissioned him, stressing that his apostleship is not due to human appointment or self-appointment (1 Cor. 1:1; 2 Cor. 1:1; Eph. 1:1; Col. 1:1).

**according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus.** The role of the apostle is to proclaim the life that is found in Christ alone (1 Tim. 1:16 note).

See Introduction to 1 Timothy: Date and Occasion; 1 Cor. 4:17 (cf. note 1 Tim. 1:2).

**Grace ... our Lord.** See note 1 Tim. 1:2.

As in most of his letters (the exceptions are Galatians, 1 Timothy, and Titus), Paul follows his salutation with a section giving thanks to God for the recipients of the letter. Here he focuses on his relationship with Timothy and his confidence in Timothy’s faith.

Probably the tears Timothy shed the last time Paul left him.

**I long to see you.** Paul anticipates his request in 4:9, 21.

These women are named only here in the NT. They were Jewish, unlike Timothy’s father, a Greek, who apparently had not allowed Eunice to have their son circumcised in infancy (Acts 16:1–3). Nonetheless, Timothy had been taught the sacred Scriptures “from childhood” (3:15), and the seed of God’s Word had flourished in Timothy’s heart as Paul brought the news of Jesus the Messiah to Lystra. See Introduction to 1 Timothy: Date and Occasion.

Paul moves into the body of the letter. As he exhorts Timothy to boldness and faithfulness, Paul discusses the gospel and his own role in proclaiming it.

**1:6 fan into flame the gift of God.** This strong expression suggests that Timothy was being less forceful than he should have been in using the spiritual gift God had given him (1 Tim. 4:14).

**laying on of my hands.** See note 1 Tim. 1:18; 4:14; 5:22.
Or, “cowardice.” This strong expression was necessary, given Timothy’s natural timidity and the gravity of his situation.
Paul is in prison in Rome (2:9; cf. Introduction: Date and Occasion).

The goal of God’s election and calling is the sanctification of His people (Eph. 1:4).

**not ... grace.** This is a marvelous affirmation that salvation is by grace, not by human merit (Eph. 2:8, 9; see Titus 3:4–6).

**because of his own purpose.** God’s decree and work of redemption is based solely on His own purpose and good pleasure. Elsewhere, this divine purpose is identified in terms of mercy (Titus 3:5) and love (Eph. 1:4, 5).

**before the ages began.** An affirmation that the divine decree of redemption through Christ is from eternity (Eph. 1:4; Titus 1:2; 1 Pet. 1:20; Rev. 13:8). In this way, Paul underscores this point that our redemption is entirely of grace and not at all in response to or grounded upon our efforts.

Elsewhere Paul consistently applies this term to Jesus’ second coming at the end of history (4:1, 8; 1 Tim. 6:14; Titus 2:13), but here it refers to His incarnation in His first coming.

**our Savior Christ Jesus.** Christ is the Mediator of the covenant of grace (Titus 1:4; 2:13; 3:6).

**who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light.** That is, through His death and resurrection (Heb. 2:14, 15; Rev. 1:18).
See 1 Tim. 2:7.

Paul is in prison (v. 8; 2:9). Paul’s entire ministry has been characterized by suffering for Christ (Acts 9:16; 2 Cor. 11:23–33).

**I am not ashamed.** Having exhorted Timothy not to be ashamed to speak out for Christ (v. 8), Paul presents himself as a model of boldness in the face of suffering (2:8–10; 3:10, 11). The gospel is folly to a perishing world, but God’s servants are not ashamed of the gospel because it is the very wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:18–2:5; Rom. 1:16, 17). He had asked for the churches’ prayers, that he might not be ashamed of Christ and His gospel but present it boldly in the highest court of the empire (Phil. 1:19, 20; Eph. 6:19, 20). Now, in his second imprisonment at Rome, their prayers are still being answered.

**that Day.** Judgment Day (v. 18; 4:8).

**what has been entrusted to me.** This relative clause reflects the concise Gk. expression, “my deposit,” as a reference to the gospel of which Paul has been a steward and trustee. As he completes his own race, Paul knows that God will guard His own word from loss or distortion. Since God will do so by means of His messengers, Paul also charges Timothy, using the same term, to “guard the good deposit entrusted to you” (v. 14).

This theme runs throughout the Pastoral Letters (1 Tim. 1:10 note; 6:3; Titus 1:9; 2:1), although only here does Paul indicate that these health-imparting words are arranged in a “pattern”—a system of interlocking and related truths.

verse_quote: the good deposit entrusted to you.
note: See v. 12 and note on 1 Tim. 6:20.

Paul’s concern that Timothy be faithful leads him to set forth specific examples of unfaithfulness and faithfulness.

**1:15 all.** Paul is probably writing with intentional exaggeration to make sure his readers see the extent of the disloyalty. At the same time, he later expresses his distress over being virtually alone, through a combination of desertion (Demas, 4:10; others, 4:16) and the deployment of faithful colleagues to other places (Crescens, Titus, Tychicus, 4:10, 12).

**Asia.** A Roman province across the Aegean Sea from Greece and today part of western Turkey. Ephesus, where Timothy was serving as Paul’s representative, was the leading city of this province.

**Phygelus and Hermogenes.** Not mentioned elsewhere in the NT. Probably Paul mentions them because he had counted on their support.

A member of the church at Ephesus who distinguished himself through his loyalty to Paul (v. 18; cf. 4:19). His proactive readiness, upon arriving at Rome, to find and serve Paul without shame, despite the apostle’s chains, is a salutary example for Paul’s beloved child Timothy (see v. 8).
Onesiphorus may have come to Rome specifically to aid Paul, as Epaphroditus had earlier traveled there on behalf of the Philippian church (Phil. 2:25–30; 4:18).
The day of judgment (v. 12; 4:8).

Paul again exhorts Timothy to be faithful, beginning with three analogies from everyday life that emphasize wholehearted devotion to a task.

**2:1 my child.** See note on 1:2.

This statement may therefore refer to Timothy’s ordination through the laying on of hands by Paul and a gathering of elders (1:6; 1 Tim. 1:18; 4:14).

**faithful men who will be able to teach others.** Presumably bishops (overseers), that is, elders (1 Tim. 3:1 note; 5:17; cf. Titus 1:7 note).

–**7** Paul draws analogies to Timothy’s ministry to Christ from three spheres of vocation: military life (vv. 3, 4), athletics (v. 5), and farming (v. 6). Then he summons Timothy to meditate on the implications of these illustrations (v. 7).

**2:3, 4 A good soldier of Christ Jesus.** Readiness to suffer, loyalty, and a single-minded commitment to please one’s commander are demanded of Christ’s soldiers. For Paul’s other uses of military metaphors for the Christian life, see 4:7; Rom. 13:12, 14; 1 Cor. 9:7; 2 Cor. 6:7; 10:4; Eph. 6:10–20; Phil. 1:27; 2:25; 4:3; 1 Tim. 1:18; 6:12; Philem. 2.
These athletic and farming analogies add a promise of future reward, which is the consummation of our salvation in our glorification (vv. 10–12)., 6

The resurrection of Christ is at the center of Paul’s theology (Rom. 4:25; Rom. 6:4–10; 1 Cor. 15:12–22). It is the basis for the hope expressed in vv. 11, 12.

**the offspring of David.** Jesus fulfills God’s promise to grant to one of David’s descendants an eternal kingship (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Matt. 1:1; Mark 12:35; Luke 1:32, 33; John 7:42; Acts 2:30–36; 13:22, 23; Rev. 5:5). For the association of Christ’s resurrection and His descent from David, see Rom. 1:3, 4.

See note on 1:8.

**the word of God is not bound.** In his prior imprisonment, Paul saw his chains actually advance the gospel of Christ (Phil. 1:12–14). Though under house arrest, he spoke the Word “without hindrance” to all who visited him (Acts 28:31).

Those whom God has chosen from before the foundation of the world to be saved (Titus 1:1).

**the salvation that is in Christ Jesus.** The salvation that comes through faith in Christ (3:15). See theological note “Salvation” on p. 2058.

**eternal glory.** This glory is the final, complete salvation of the elect in the new order of God. The saints will have resurrection bodies and transformed human natures (1 Cor. 15:42–49). They will experience fully the triumph of Christ over sin and death, and know fullness of joy in a life secured for them by Christ’s death, resurrection, and ascension (v. 11; Matt. 13:43; 1 Tim. 1:16 note; cf. Ps. 16:11).

See note on 1 Tim. 1:15. What follows may be part of an early Christian hymn.

**If we have died with him.** A reference to the believer’s union with Christ in His death on the cross (Rom. 6:3–11).

This refers to perseverance in the face of hardship (v. 10).

**we will also reign with him.** A NT image for the eternal glory that Christians receive through Christ (Matt. 19:28; Rom. 5:17; Rev. 3:21; 5:10; 20:4, 6; 22:5).

**if we deny him, he also will deny us.** A sober warning against apostasy, grounded in the words of Jesus Himself (Matt. 10:33).

verse_quote: if we are faithless, he remains faithful.
note:
This is a wonderful affirmation of assurance that although we are called to endure and be faithful, salvation does not rest ultimately on our faithfulness, but upon the perfect faithfulness of Christ (v. 19).

**he cannot deny himself.** Christian hope is rooted firmly in the unchanging character of God (Num. 23:19; Titus 1:2) and His unchangeable redemptive purpose for His elect (Heb. 6:13–20).
One of the characteristics of the false teachers (v. 23; 1 Tim. 1:4; 6:4; Titus 3:9). False teaching “only ruins the hearers,” but sound doctrine alone can save and restore its hearers.
The whole counsel of God, with emphasis upon the gospel (2:8, 9; 4:2).

Mentioned also in 1 Tim. 1:19, 20 as one who has made “shipwreck” of his faith.

**Philetus.** Mentioned nowhere else in the NT.

This false belief denied the future bodily resurrection of Christians and affirmed instead that a spiritual resurrection at conversion was the sum total of the Christian’s resurrection. Thus, this false belief resulted in an overemphasis on present experience (1 Cor. 15:12–14). Furthermore, to deny a final bodily resurrection is to deny that there is a final reversal of Adam’s sin, which not only introduced spiritual death but also physical death. Thus, it is to deny a final salvation of the whole person in an eternal new creation. Consequently, such a teaching is heresy.

**They are upsetting the faith of some.** The doctrines of the false teachers are at odds with the gospel. Timothy must warn the church about them (v. 14).

This statement is a reference to God’s elect (cf. 2:10; Titus 1:1).

**stands.** In contrast to those who wander away (v. 18).

**seal.** An expression of ownership and security.

**The Lord knows those who are his.** A quotation of Num. 16:5 (according to the Septuagint). In the OT context, Korah and other rebels insisted that they had the right to demand access to God’s presence, but the Lord reasserted His sovereign right to choose Aaron as His high priest to draw near in His most holy place. Inscribed on the people of God is His eternal decree of election (v. 11), which ensures the security of the body of Christ (John 10:29).

**Let everyone ... depart.** Perhaps also inscribed on the membership of God’s people is His call to holiness (v. 21), including the repudiation of false teaching. Paul may be paraphrasing, from the same OT context, God’s summons to the Israelites to keep their distance from Korah and his comrades (Num. 16:26). In accordance with the Num. 16:26 allusion, the idea is that the false teachers are being exhorted to “depart” from their false teaching (perhaps in line with and developed in 2:25, 26).
These verses provide an example from everyday life of the importance of holiness—being set apart for a noble (godly) task., 21
See note on 2:14; 1 Tim. 1:3, 4, 6, 7.

This title evokes the image of the servant of the Lord in Isaiah, who treats the bruised reed and smoldering wick with gentleness (Is. 42:1–3, applied to Jesus in Matt. 12:15–21). See also Matt. 11:28–30. Jesus’ patience and kindness in response to obstinate opponents project the pattern for those who teach His church.

The Christian must never assume that those who are ensnared by the devil’s false teaching are irretrievably lost. The gospel must be proclaimed to all. Notice Paul’s concern for the manner in which Timothy is to engage his opponents—with kindness, patience, gentleness, and the other fruit of the Holy Spirit (cf. Gal. 5:22)., 26

Paul continues on the theme of false teaching by turning to an attack on the false teachers themselves, noting their impact upon the church at Ephesus, but concluding with the affirmation that they will not succeed in the end.

**3:1 the last days.** The era inaugurated by Christ’s first advent and completed by His second (1 Tim. 4:1 note).

verse_quote: having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power.
note: What makes the false teachers so dangerous is that they appear to be Christians (Matt. 7:15, 21–23).

Paul’s point is not that all women are this way, but that some have been especially vulnerable to deception. The false teachers at Ephesus had been especially successful in deceiving women (1 Tim. 2:14; 5:13–15).

According to Jewish tradition, these are the names of two of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses before Pharaoh (Ex. 7; 8). Paul’s inclusion of these names in his second letter to Timothy indicates that this Jewish tradition reflects actual history.

With the problem of the false teachers fully in view, Paul once more turns to exhorting Timothy to faithfulness, first in terms of the example that Paul has set (and implicitly that of Timothy’s mother and grandmother), and then in terms of confidence in and obedience to Scripture.

**3:10, 11** Once again, Paul appeals to his own life, both his faithfulness and his sufferings, as an example for Timothy (1:11–13; 2:8–10).

**3:11 Antioch ... Iconium ... Lystra.** Three cities in the Roman province of Galatia where Paul preached the gospel on his first missionary journey (Acts 13:14–14:20). Against significant opposition, Paul succeeded in establishing a church in each city (Acts 14:21–23). Paul mentions these cities, including Timothy’s home of Lystra, in order to appeal to the roots of Timothy’s faith (vv. 14, 15; 1:5). Since Timothy’s maturity was evident to the church when Paul and Silas reached Lystra on Paul’s second journey (Acts 16:2), it appears that Timothy, his mother, Eunice, and his grandmother Lois had come to faith in Jesus the Messiah as a result of that first journey (1:5).

**the Lord rescued me.** Paul was stoned and left for dead at Lystra, but God revived him (Acts 14:19). See 4:18 and note.

verse_quote: all who desire to live a godly life ... will be persecuted.
note: The NT teaches that Christians should expect persecution and should not be surprised when it comes upon them as they pursue godliness (Matt. 10:17, 18; John 15:20; 1 Pet. 4:12; 5:9). This was the apostles’ consistent message when encouraging newly converted believers in newly planted churches (Acts 14:22).
A reference to Timothy’s mother and grandmother (1:5), as well as to Paul himself.

According to custom, the Jewish parent was to begin instructing a child in the law when the child reached five years old.

**you have been acquainted with the sacred writings.** The false teachers have been misinterpreting the OT (1 Tim. 1:7; Titus 3:9). Timothy needs to remember the proper instruction he received at the hands of his mother and grandmother. The “sacred writings” here are the books of the OT. The NT did not yet exist as a complete collection. Indeed, some of the NT books had not yet been written.

**salvation ... in Christ Jesus.** The OT, interpreted properly, leads one to understand the central role of Jesus Christ in God’s overall plan for His creation (Luke 24:25–27, 44–49; John 5:45–47). This fact confirms both the error and danger of the false teachers’ mishandling of the OT law.

The OT (v. 15 note).

**breathed out by God.** This is one of the most important expressions in the NT of the doctrine of the divine inspiration of Scripture. The Bible has been breathed out by the Spirit of God (2 Pet. 1:21). God is the source and ultimate author of Scripture. Though written by human authors, Scripture nevertheless has the full weight of His authority. The Bible, from start to finish and down to its very words, is the inerrant Word of God.

The great American Reformed theologian, B.B. Warfield, who taught at Princeton Theological Seminary from 1887–1921, demonstrated that the Gk. term translated “breathed out by God” (_theopneustos_) refers to all of Scripture and not just portions of it. In other words, the entirety of the canon of Scripture, down to the individual words themselves, were given by God and therefore entirely true. The Bible affirms no errors and is the only infallible source of Christian doctrine.

Paul brings to a conclusion the appeal to Timothy begun in 1:6.

**4:1 in the presence of God.** Paul mentions witnesses to impress on Timothy the utmost seriousness of the charge, just as elsewhere he invokes God as a witness to emphasize the truth of his assertions (Rom 1:9; 9:1; 2 Cor. 1:23; Phil. 1:8; 1 Thess. 2:5).

**Christ Jesus, who is to judge.** For Christ as the Judge of all, see v. 8; Matt. 25:31–46; John 5:22, 27; Acts 10:42.

**his appearing.** Christ’s second coming (cf. v. 8; 1 Tim. 6:14; Titus 2:13).

The whole Word of God, with emphasis upon the gospel (cf. 2:15).

**in season and out of season.** In every situation, whether good or bad, the Word is to be proclaimed.

See note on 1:13.

**itching ears.** Some people have an endless fascination with everything but the truth. They look for and attract false teachers to themselves.

**they.** Presumably a reference to some who are associated with the church.
See note on 1 Tim. 1:4.

A final exhortation to faithfulness, even though others may be turning away.

**the work of an evangelist.** One who announces good news (the _evangel_, or gospel), particularly to those not yet converted. In Eph. 4:11, evangelists are listed alongside apostles, prophets, shepherds, and teachers as those who bring God’s Word. Philip, first ordained to care for widows’ material needs, was later sent out to proclaim the gospel in Samaria, to an Ethiopian, and in coastal towns; thus, he is also called an evangelist (Acts 21:8).

Paul’s impending death provides the reason for his extended appeal to Timothy (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

**4:6 already.** Paul accepts the inevitability of his death, even if it may still be several months away. His sense of completion in this second imprisonment differs markedly from his expectation of release to carry on further ministry when he wrote Philippians (Phil. 1:24–26; 2:24).

**poured out as a drink offering.** This metaphor for death (cf. Phil. 2:17) is taken from the language of the OT sacrificial system. A drink offering of wine was poured out in the sanctuary as an offering to God (Num. 15:5, 7, 10; 28:7). Paul understands his impending death as an offering to Christ.

**my departure.** Another metaphor for death (Phil. 1:23). Paul held steadfastly to the hope and assurance of a destination beyond the grave (v. 18; cf. Phil. 2:21–23).

With these three metaphors, Paul signifies the end of his ministry. His concern is not that he has been a success, but rather that he has been faithful to his Lord. He has exhorted Timothy through similar metaphors to be faithful (1 Tim. 6:12; 2 Tim. 2:4).

Perhaps the crown awarded for the faithful life of one who has received the righteousness of Christ through faith (Rom. 3:22). More likely, this is the crown consisting of perfect righteousness—eternal life that is given to the believer as the climax of the process of sanctification (2:10; James 1:12; 1 Pet. 5:4; Rev. 2:10).

**the righteous judge.** Christ in His role as the divine Judge who brings to completion the work He has begun in His elect.

**that Day.** Judgment day (1:12, 18).

**his appearing.** Christ’s second coming (v. 1).

Paul now turns to his primary reason for writing the letter: he wants to see Timothy one last time. Paul gives Timothy various instructions regarding his journey to Rome, informs Timothy of his present status, and concludes with a profound expression of trust in his Lord.

**4:9 Do your best to come to me.** Paul hinted at his desire to see Timothy in 1:4.

**soon.** See note on v. 21.

A coworker present with Paul during his first Roman imprisonment (Col. 4:14; Philem. 24).

**Thessalonica.** A city in the Roman province of Macedonia where Paul had established a church on his second missionary journey (Acts 17:1–10).

**Crescens.** Mentioned nowhere else in the NT, he was apparently another of Paul’s coworkers.

**Galatia.** Either a Roman province Paul visited on his first missionary journey (3:11 note), or a region in Asia Minor that Paul visited on his second missionary journey (Acts 16: 6).

**Titus.** Another of Paul’s coworkers. See Introduction to Titus: Date and Occasion.

**Dalmatia.** Another name for the Roman province of Illyricum, the westernmost province reached by Paul on his first three missionary journeys (Rom. 15:19).

The “beloved physician,” mentioned in Col. 4:14 and Philem. 24, who traveled with Paul throughout much of his second and third missionary journeys (Introduction to Luke: Author).

**Get Mark and bring him with you.** A beautiful example of Christian forgiveness and restoration. John Mark’s desertion of Paul and Barnabas during their first missionary journey (Acts 13:13) had occasioned the dissolution of the partnership between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37–39). Later, Mark regained Paul’s favor (Col. 4:10; Philem. 24). Now, at the end of his life, Paul wants to see him, “for he is very useful.”

The coworker of Paul, mentioned in Acts 20:4 and Titus 3:12, who carried Paul’s epistles to the churches in Ephesus and Colossae during Paul’s first Roman imprisonment (Eph. 6:21; Col. 4:7).

**to Ephesus.** Tychicus is to take this letter to Timothy and serve as his replacement.

A heavy woolen garment used for protection against dampness and cold. Paul is anticipating the arrival of winter (v. 21).

**Carpus.** Mentioned nowhere else in the NT.

**Troas.** A port linking the Roman province of Asia with Macedonia across the Aegean Sea (Acts 16:7, 8 note). Paul had traveled through Troas on his second and third missionary journeys (Acts 16:8, 11; 20:5, 6). When Paul was in Troas on this fourth and final journey is not clear. This may have been the place where Paul was arrested and from where he was transported to Rome.

**books.** Likely materials for writing to the churches and/or copies of Paul’s writings that he had already sent to his coworkers and the churches under his care.

**parchments.** Parchment is a writing material made from the skins of animals, especially sheep or goats. It is significantly more durable than papyrus. Probably Paul was asking for parts of the OT.

See note on 1 Tim. 1:20.

**did me great harm.** This incident is mentioned nowhere else in the NT.

**the Lord will repay him according to his deeds.** That is, on the day of final judgment (Matt. 16:27; Rom. 2:6; Rev. 22:12).

A preliminary hearing before Paul’s actual trial, which he now awaits (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

**May it not be charged against them.** An expression of forgiveness in the face of death reminiscent of Christ (Luke 23:34) and of Stephen (Acts 7:60), whose death Paul had witnessed and approved of in his years of unbelief (Acts 7:58; 8:1).

verse_quote: But the Lord stood by me.
note:
Paul had learned long ago that he could always depend upon the one who had commissioned him (2 Cor. 12:9, 10; Phil. 4:11–13).

**the message might be fully proclaimed.** This probably refers to Paul’s proclamation of the gospel at his preliminary hearing.

**all the Gentiles might hear.** Paul had preached the gospel in a public forum at the center of the Roman Empire.

**rescued from the lion’s mouth.** A metaphor for a narrow escape from death, perhaps alluding to Daniel’s deliverance from actual lions (Dan. 6). Paul’s preliminary hearing resulted in a temporary reprieve. See note on 1 Cor. 15:32.

verse_quote: will rescue me from every evil deed.
note:
Paul does not believe that Christ will prevent his physical death (v. 6), but is expressing his absolute trust in Christ (2:13) as the one who purposes to overrule evil for His glory and for the good of His servants.

**bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom.** This is the ultimate hope of all who trust in Christ. Death, far from keeping Paul from Christ’s kingdom, is the very means of his entrance into the fullness of the blessings of Christ’s spiritual kingdom.

As is his custom, Paul closes the letter with personal greetings and a benediction.

**4:19 Prisca and Aquila.** “Prisca” is a shortened form of “Priscilla,” as it is spelled elsewhere in Acts and Paul’s letters. She and her husband, Aquila, had been friends of Paul from the time he first visited Corinth on his second missionary journey. They were Jews, and like Paul were tentmakers (Acts 18:2, 3). They had come to Corinth from Rome. Later, they accompanied Paul to Ephesus (Acts 18:18, 19) and hosted a church in their home there for several years before returning to Rome (Rom. 16:3, 4; 1 Cor. 16:19). They had now apparently returned to Ephesus where Timothy was (1 Tim. 1:3).

**the household of Onesiphorus.** See note on 1:16. This greeting indicates that Timothy was still in Ephesus (1:18).

Presumably the same person as Corinth’s treasurer mentioned in Rom. 16:23.

**Corinth.** The provincial capital of the Roman province of Achaia. It was visited by Paul on his second and third missionary journeys. Corinth is fifty miles (80 km) west of Athens.

**Trophimus.** A member of the church at Ephesus who accompanied Paul to Jerusalem at the close of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:4; 21:29).

**Miletus.** A seaport just south of Ephesus, which Paul visited at the end of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:15, 17). When Paul visited Miletus on his fourth and final journey is not clear.

Winter weather would prevent travel by ship (see Acts 27:9–12; 28:11). Paul may have felt that if Timothy waited too long, he would not arrive before Paul’s execution (v. 9). In any event, he needed his cloak before winter (v. 13).

**Eubulus ... Pudens and Linus and Claudia.** These were Christians in Rome, although none is mentioned elsewhere in the NT.
The Gk. word for “you” is plural (text note). Presumably, Paul intended the letter to be read to the entire church (1 Tim. 6:21 note; Titus 3:15).
